title: The big picture
text: Introduction to stochastic calculus A little noise.A different calculus. Start with motion you can predict. Then ask what changes when each step becomes uncertain.
excerpt: Introduction to stochastic calculus

title: First, a predictable journey
text: Imagine an object moving along a straight line at a constant speed. If we know where it starts and how fast it moves, we can predict where it will be: x(t)=x_0+vt. Every second adds the same displacement. Repeating the experiment under the same idealized rule gives the same line. Ordinary calculus helps us describe such motion even when the speed varies.
excerpt: Imagine an object moving along a straight line at a constant speed.

title: Now make the steps uncertain
text: Suppose small disturbances sometimes push the object a little farther right and sometimes left. The steady part of its motion is still useful, but it no longer determines the exact position. Repeating the experiment produces different paths. We now want to answer two questions: what does one possible journey look like, and how are the possible destinations distributed? Stochastic calculus develops tools for describing change with this kind of uncertainty.
excerpt: Suppose small disturbances sometimes push the object a little farther right and sometimes left.

title: Now make the steps uncertain
text: To begin, set the steady motion aside and isolate the disturbances. Replace all their physical complexity with one simple rule: at each step a fair coin chooses a push to the right or left. Heads means right; tails means left. A sequence of tosses then becomes a random walk. This is a deliberately simplified model that we can count and understand before taking a continuous limit.
excerpt: To begin, set the steady motion aside and isolate the disturbances.

title: Why study this?
text: Physics: many unresolved molecular collisions make the position of a tiny suspended particle uncertain. We want to describe how a cloud of particles spreads. Finance: a price model describes a range of possible future values. Connecting those models to option pricing requires a calculus for random changes. Biology: diffusion helps describe molecules moving through a cell. Machine learning: some generative models learn how to reverse a process that gradually adds noise to data. The core chapters here develop the stochastic calculus needed to understand such models.
excerpt: Physics: many unresolved molecular collisions make the position of a tiny suspended particle uncertain.

title: Why study this?
text: We will start with coins, count their possible paths, and ask how very many small steps become a continuous process. That will reveal why ordinary calculus needs one extra term. Assumed background: basic calculus, averages, and variance. This interactive lesson is based on Ji-Ha Kim’s Introduction to Stochastic Calculus, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Our explanations, derivations, and experiments adapt and extend that foundation. See the source attribution and description of changes.
excerpt: We will start with coins, count their possible paths, and ask how very many small steps become a continuous process.

title: From a coin toss to a step
text: Take the left/right disturbance from the introduction. Draw a number line and start at zero. Moving right increases the coordinate by one; moving left decreases it by one: Heads (H) Right → +1 Tails (T) Left ← -1 For example, H, T, H gives positions 0\to1\to0\to1. The changes are +1,-1,+1, and their sum is the final position +1. For now the coin is fair, and each toss is independent of the earlier tosses. The coin stands in for an uncertain kick. It is not a claim that molecules literally toss coins. Its value is that we can list every possibility and ask how a repeated local rule builds a path.
excerpt: Take the left/right disturbance from the introduction.

title: One toss. One step.
context: Interactive simulation experiment. From a coin toss to a step
text: Heads moves right: +1. Tails moves left: −1. Add up to twelve tosses and follow the position. Try this. Reveal three tosses. Write down the route and final position. Could another order of the same heads and tails reach the same endpoint? A fair independent coin model, simulated with seeded draws. “Replay this sequence” clears the revealed steps and lets you reveal the same outcomes again. “Draw a new sequence” selects a fresh set of outcomes and returns to the start; its sequence number changes. Next, count all possible routes instead of watching only one.
excerpt: Heads moves right: +1.

title: Counting routes with Pascal’s triangle
text: After one step there are two possible positions. After two steps, right-then-left and left-then-right both return to zero. At every later step, the number of ways to reach a node is the sum of the numbers at its two parent nodes: \begin{array}{ccccccc}&&&1&&&\\&&1&&1&&\\&1&&2&&1&\\1&&3&&3&&1\end{array} These are the first four rows of Pascal’s triangle. Using zero-based indexing, row n counts paths after n steps. Its entry k counts paths with k right steps: \binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}, k=0,1,\ldots,n. For three steps and two right moves, the routes are RRL, RLR, and LRR. There are \binom32=3 of them. Each ends at position +1, but follows a different intermediate path.
excerpt: After one step there are two possible positions.

title: From route counts to probabilities
text: We will use three statistical symbols: \mathbb P means probability, \mathbb E means the average over many repetitions, and Var measures the average squared distance from that average. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and gives a spread in the same units as position. Now allow a biased coin: the probability of a right step is p, and of a left step is q=1-p. Under independence, probabilities multiply. Any particular sequence containing k right moves and n-k left moves has probability p^kq^{n-k}. Multiplying by the number of such sequences gives the binomial law: \mathbb P(K=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
excerpt: We will use three statistical symbols: \(\mathbb P\) means probability, \(\mathbb E\) means the average over many repetitions, and \(\operatorname{Var}\) measures the average squared distance from that average.

title: From route counts to probabilities
text: Here K counts right moves. Position is a different variable: subtract the number of left moves from the number of right moves: S_n=(+1)K+(-1)(n-K)=2K-n. For example, with three fair tosses the probability of ending at +1 is 3(1/2)^3=3/8. The endpoints lie on a lattice; probability mass at a reachable position is not a continuous probability density.
excerpt: Here \(K\) counts right moves.

title: A pattern from coin flips
context: Interactive simulation experiment. From route counts to probabilities
text: Compare the exact binomial probabilities with repeated simulated walks. Try this. Set n=3 and p=0.5. The exact mass at +1 is 3/8. Then increase p: the center moves right, while the route counts stay the same. Each line is one sample walk. Green lines can overlap and look darker, but shade is not a calibrated path count or probability. Use the endpoint bars to compare frequencies. Bars show probability mass at the reachable lattice positions, not a continuous density. Changing a control reuses the same seeded random numbers.
excerpt: Compare the exact binomial probabilities with repeated simulated walks.

title: Separate a trend from its fluctuations
text: Set the right-step probability in the graph to 75%. Each toss still moves exactly one unit. Yet the dashed line rises by half a unit per toss: 0.75(+1)+0.25(-1)=0.5. How can the average step be a step the walker never takes? Imagine four moves containing three heads and one tail. They gain two units altogether, or half a unit per move. Individual runs need not contain those exact counts.
excerpt: Set the right-step probability in the graph to 75%.

title: Separate a trend from its fluctuations
text: The dashed line describes the average over repetitions; the blue walk shows the departures from that average. A right step lies +0.5 above the predicted change; a left step misses it by -1.5. Their weighted average is zero. We can do this bookkeeping for any step length. For spatial steps Δ X_i\in\{-Δ x,+Δ x\}, compute the mean of one step: m:=\mathbb E[Δ X_i]=(p-q)Δ x=(2p-1)Δ x. Adding and subtracting that mean splits an individual step into a systematic part and a centered random part: Δ X_i=\underbrace{m}_{mean step}+\underbrace{(Δ X_i-m)}_{zero-mean fluctuation}.
excerpt: The dashed line describes the average over repetitions; the blue walk shows the departures from that average.

title: Separate a trend from its fluctuations
text: The centered part of a biased two-point step need not be symmetric. What matters here is that its expectation is zero. Its variance follows from \mathbb E[(Δ X_i)^2]=(Δ x)^2: Var(Δ X_i)=(Δ x)^2-m^2=4p(1-p)(Δ x)^2. For independent steps, means and variances add. With unit steps, \mathbb E[S_n]=n(2p-1) and Var(S_n)=4np(1-p). These describe an ensemble of walks, not the destination of every individual walk.
excerpt: The centered part of a biased two-point step need not be symmetric.

title: Why local rules lead beyond the binomial formula
text: So far you have changed one slider for the entire walk. What if the walker changes the coin at each location? Try a rule on paper: heads has probability 1/2 at zero, 1/4 to its right, and 1/2 to its left. Right–left returns to zero with probability (1/2)(3/4)=3/8; left–right also returns to zero, but with probability (1/2)(1/2)=1/4. The route count is still two. Multiplying it by a single route probability no longer works.
excerpt: So far you have changed one slider for the entire walk.

title: Why local rules lead beyond the binomial formula
text: The binomial expression relies on the same step size and probability at every trial. If a restoring force makes a rightward position favor leftward steps, a route’s probability depends on the intermediate positions. Two routes can still meet, but no longer have equal probabilities merely because their right-step counts agree. In a price model, the size of a fluctuation may instead grow with the current price. The local rule now depends on the state. We can describe that rule even when one global path-counting formula is unavailable. This is the motivation for differential equations with random input. Assess the assumption.
excerpt: The binomial expression relies on the same step size and probability at every trial.

title: Why local rules lead beyond the binomial formula
text: Independence is a modeling choice. A streak alone does not prove dependence, and a model’s usefulness must be checked against the system or data it is meant to describe. Before letting the rule depend on location, let’s give the fair walk a clock. If we fit twice as many tosses into one second, how far should each toss move us?
excerpt: Independence is a modeling choice.

title: Why local rules lead beyond the binomial formula
context: Pause for a prediction
text: Does a fair coin mean every walk finishes at zero? See the reasoning No. It means the expected endpoint is zero. Individual endpoints differ; zero is not even reachable after an odd number of unit steps.
excerpt: Does a fair coin mean every walk finishes at zero?

title: One destination is not yet a whole journey
text: Section 2 described a walk one coin toss at a time. Now imagine making more and more steps within the same amount of physical time. Can the increasingly detailed walk approach a useful continuous model? First recall what we know about its final position. Let \xi_i be the direction of toss i: heads gives +1, tails gives -1. The position after n unit steps is: S_n=\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_n. A fair step has mean zero and variance one. Because the steps are independent, the sum has mean zero and variance n. Its standard deviation—its typical spread around the mean—is therefore √ n. Dividing by that spread gives a quantity with variance one: \mathbb E[S_n]=0, Var (\frac{S_n}{√ n} )=1.
excerpt: Section 2 described a walk one coin toss at a time.

title: One destination is not yet a whole journey
text: The central limit theorem says that the distribution of S_n/√ n approaches a standard normal bell curve as n grows. In symbols: \frac{S_n}{√ n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1). The arrow means that the distribution approaches the normal distribution. It does not say that a particular walk's endpoint approaches a fixed number. The notation \mathcal N(0,1) denotes a normal distribution with mean zero and variance one, hence standard deviation one. But this still describes only one chosen observation: the destination at the end. For example, a bell curve for the position at one second says nothing by itself about where the same walker was at a quarter-second or a half-second.
excerpt: The central limit theorem says that the distribution of \(S_n/\sqrt n\) approaches a standard normal bell curve as \(n\) grows.

title: One destination is not yet a whole journey
text: A random variable gives one uncertain number per repetition, such as the final position. To describe the journey, we need a random position for every time and a rule connecting those positions into a path. That time-indexed collection is called a stochastic process. Our next task is to attach a clock and a distance scale to the coin walk.
excerpt: A random variable gives one uncertain number per repetition, such as the final position.

title: Give the walk a clock and a step length
text: Fix the total duration at T, and arrange n equally spaced tosses. The time step is the time between consecutive tosses: Δ t=\frac{T}{n}. The symbol Δ x is the distance moved by each toss. These are different quantities: Δ t is a duration; Δ x is a length. For a one-second walk with 100 tosses, the time step is 0.01 seconds. At an observation time t, how many tosses have happened? Divide elapsed time by the time step and round down to count completed steps: m(t)= \lfloor\frac{t}{Δ t} \rfloor. The floor brackets mean “round down.” For instance, if a toss occurs every 0.1 seconds, then by t=0.35 seconds three tosses have happened.
excerpt: Fix the total duration at \(T\), and arrange \(n\) equally spaced tosses.

title: Give the walk a clock and a step length
context: Build the position by adding the completed moves
text: Toss i moves the particle by Δ x \xi_i: either +Δ x or -Δ x. Starting at zero, add the moves completed by time t: \begin{aligned}W_{Δ t}(t)&=Δ x \xi_1+\cdots+Δ x \xi_{m(t)}\\&=Δ x\sum_{i=1}^{m(t)}\xi_i.\end{aligned} Read the notation: W_{Δ t}(t) means “the position at time t of the walk built using time step Δ t.” The subscript labels which time grid we chose. It is not multiplication by Δ t, a derivative, or the size of a move. Each smaller time step gives a different, finer approximation.
excerpt: Toss \(i\) moves the particle by \(\Delta x\,\xi_i\): either \(+\Delta x\) or \(-\Delta x\).

title: Give the walk a clock and a step length
context: Derive its variance, one step at a time
text: Multiplying a random variable by Δ x multiplies its variance by (Δ x)^2. Since Var(\xi_i)=1, one physical step has variance (Δ x)^2. Independent variances add, so: \begin{aligned}Var(W_{Δ t}(t))&=\sum_{i=1}^{m(t)}Var(Δ x \xi_i)\\&=m(t)(Δ x)^2\\&= \lfloor\frac{t}{Δ t} \rfloor(Δ x)^2.\end{aligned} For example, take T=1, n=100, and Δ x=0.1. At t=0.37, there have been 37 moves. Their position variance is 37\times0.1^2=0.37. At one second it is 100\times0.1^2=1. When t lies exactly on the grid, there is no rounding, and the variance is t(Δ x)^2/Δ t. To preserve a finite amount of uncertainty while fitting more tosses into the same duration, we must choose how the spatial step shrinks with the time step.
excerpt: Multiplying a random variable by \(\Delta x\) multiplies its variance by \((\Delta x)^2\).

title: Give the walk a clock and a step length
context: Derive its variance, one step at a time
text: Keep Δ x=1 t/Δ t Spreads without bound: more full-size kicks. Choose Δ x=Δ t tΔ t Collapses toward zero: the random kicks shrink too quickly. Choose Δ x=√{Δ t} t Keeps the same spread at the same physical time. This is why the square root appears: independent squared step sizes accumulate. We need (Δ x)^2 to shrink at the same rate as Δ t. A constant multiplier σ is also possible: Δ x=σ√{Δ t} gives variance σ^2t. The experiment shows the endpoint distribution as bars. Their areas represent fractions of all sampled walks; height alone is a density, not a probability. The smooth bell curve approximates those discrete endpoints. Its horizontal width shows the spread.
excerpt: Keep \(\Delta x=1\) \(t/\Delta t\) Spreads without bound: more full-size kicks.

context: Derive its variance, one step at a time
text: Two fixed windows make the comparison visible: use the close view to see a cloud shrink toward zero and the wide view to see it spread outward. Neither horizontal axis zooms when you change the controls.
excerpt: Two fixed windows make the comparison visible: use the close view to see a cloud shrink toward zero and the wide view to see it spread outward.

context: Interactive simulation experiment. Give the walk a clock and a step length
text: Fit more fair coin steps into one second. See what happens when their spatial size shrinks at different rates. Paths leaving this close view are clipped at its boundary. The wide endpoint view below shows their larger spread. This horizontal window stays fixed for every choice. The same endpoints on a second, fixed horizontal scale. Try this. Choose Δ x=Δ t and increase the number of steps from 8 to 1,024: the close-view cloud contracts toward zero. Choose Δ x=1: use the wide view to see it spread. Choose √{Δ t}: its width stays about the same as the grid is refined.

title: Keep the time. Change the scale.
context: Interactive simulation experiment. Give the walk a clock and a step length
text: Each mode at a given step count uses the same coin outcomes. Across different step counts these are new finite walks, not nested samples of a single path. Bars show density: endpoint counts divided by all 2,000 walks and the bin width. Bins group an odd number of lattice positions when needed for readability. The smooth normal curve is an approximation, especially with few steps. Its horizontal width is governed by the exact standard deviation.
excerpt: Each mode at a given step count uses the same coin outcomes.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
text: Imagine a speck of dye in a stream. Its motion is irregular, but the current carries it downstream by two units per second on average. That average displacement per unit time is its drift. We want our coin walk to represent the same stream whether we divide a second into 100 steps or 400. We already know how to keep the random spread finite. How do we keep the current’s speed fixed too?
excerpt: Imagine a speck of dye in a stream.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: What goes wrong if the coin stays 60% right?
text: Start with 100 tosses in one second, each moving the speck 0.1 unit. A right move cancels a left move of the same size, so only the excess of right moves contributes to the net displacement. A 60% coin gives 60 right and 40 left on average: 20 extra right moves carry the center of the cloud 20\times0.1=2 units downstream. At this clock rate the coin works exactly as intended. Now divide each time interval into four. The square-root rule from the previous experiment says that a step lasting a quarter as long moves half as far. Follow the same one second on both clocks: 100 0.1 60-40=20 20\times0.1=2 400 0.05 240-160=80 80\times0.05=4
excerpt: Start with 100 tosses in one second, each moving the speck \(0.1\) unit.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: What goes wrong if the coin stays 60% right?
text: The coin gives us four times as many excess right moves, each still half as long. Their combined push doubles. Refine the clock by four again and the predicted drift doubles again. The stream did not speed up; our choice to keep the same preference per toss made the model speed up. The numbers in the table are averages over many walks; an individual speck can still finish upstream. Here is the same argument in symbols. A toss has mean displacement pΔ x-(1-p)Δ x=(2p-1)Δ x, and there are 1/Δ t tosses per unit time. For Δ x=√{Δ t} in our chosen units: drift rate=\frac{(2p-1)Δ x}{Δ t}=\frac{2p-1}{√{Δ t}}.
excerpt: The coin gives us four times as many excess right moves, each still half as long.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: What goes wrong if the coin stays 60% right?
text: With p=0.6, the numerator stays at 0.2 while the denominator shrinks toward zero. The mean speed therefore grows without bound. A fair coin avoids this because its numerator is zero, but it would give us no downstream current at all.
excerpt: With \(p=0.6\), the numerator stays at \(0.2\) while the denominator shrinks toward zero.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: How can the finer walk keep the same current?
text: On the 400-step clock, each step is 0.05 unit long. To travel two units on average, we need 2/0.05=40 extra right moves, not 80. A coin that lands right 55% of the time gives exactly that: 220-180=40 on average. Although this coin is closer to fair, 40\times0.05=2: it describes the same drift as the 60% coin on the coarser clock. For any desired drift μ, the mean displacement during one interval must be μΔ t. Keep the spatial step σ√{Δ t}, where σ sets the strength of the random fluctuations, and solve for the required right-step probability: \begin{aligned}(2p-1)σ√{Δ t}&=μΔ t,\\2p-1&=\frac{μ√{Δ t}}{σ},\\p&=\frac12+\frac{μ√{Δ t}}{2σ}, σ>0.\end{aligned}
excerpt: On the 400-step clock, each step is \(0.05\) unit long.

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: How can the finer walk keep the same current?
text: In our stream, μ=2 and σ=1. The formula gives p=0.60 at 100 steps per second and p=0.55 at 400, just as we found by counting. As the grid gets finer the coin approaches fair, but the drift does not disappear: a mean push of μΔ t per step, repeated 1/Δ t times, still gives μ per unit time.
excerpt: In our stream, \(\mu=2\) and \(\sigma=1\).

title: What if the walk also has a steady trend?
context: How can the finer walk keep the same current?
text: Does weakening the bias spoil the random spread we just worked to preserve? Each squared step is σ^2Δ t, and the mean step is μΔ t. Subtracting the squared mean gives a single-step variance of σ^2Δ t-μ^2(Δ t)^2. Independent steps add their variances, so the variance per unit time is σ^2-μ^2Δ t, approaching σ^2. We keep both the current and the spread. The grid must be fine enough that the calculated p lies between zero and one.
excerpt: Does weakening the bias spoil the random spread we just worked to preserve?

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
text: We have answered a mathematical question: how should we shrink independent coin steps to keep the accumulated spread finite? Now ask the modeling question: is square-root spreading actually a useful description of a physical particle? A tiny suspended particle is jostled by the surrounding fluid. Over suitable observation times, its one-dimensional mean squared displacement is modeled by: \mathbb E[(X_t-X_0)^2]=2Dt.
excerpt: We have answered a mathematical question: how should we shrink independent coin steps to keep the accumulated spread finite?

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
text: Here D is the diffusivity, which measures the spreading rate. The root-mean-square distance is √{2Dt}. So the physical diffusion model has exactly the square-root time behavior we obtained by scaling coin steps. This is the connection we wanted; it does not claim that all random motion has this scaling at every time scale.
excerpt: Here \(D\) is the diffusivity, which measures the spreading rate.

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
context: Why random kicks can produce it
text: Call the signed displacement of kick i by the name Y_i. Suppose the kicks are independent and centered at zero, with root-mean-square length \ell, meaning \mathbb E[Y_i^2]=\ell^2. For N such kicks, their squared contributions add while their cross terms average to zero: \begin{aligned}\mathbb E [ (\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i )^2 ]&=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E[Y_i^2]\\& +2\sum_{i When the number of effectively independent kicks grows in proportion to time, the mean squared displacement grows in proportion to time too. This is the same cancellation mechanism as in the fair coin walk.
excerpt: Call the signed displacement of kick \(i\) by the name \(Y_i\).

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
context: How this connects to the diffusion equation
text: Let p(x,t) be the position density of a large collection of particles. The constant-diffusivity equation is: \frac{\partial p}{\partial t}=D\frac{\partial^2p}{\partial x^2}. Its Gaussian solution, for particles all starting at zero, has variance 2Dt. This equation describes a distribution; Section 6 will instead specify the local rule for an individual random path. For spherical particles in the regime where the Stokes–Einstein relation applies, the physical parameters determine D: D=\frac{k_B\mathcal T}{6\pi\eta r}.
excerpt: Let \(p(x,t)\) be the position density of a large collection of particles.

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
context: How this connects to the diffusion equation
text: The symbols are Boltzmann's constant k_B, absolute temperature \mathcal T, viscosity \eta, and particle radius r. Einstein and Smoluchowski developed quantitative theories of this diffusion; Perrin's experiments provided important evidence for the molecular explanation.
excerpt: The symbols are Boltzmann's constant \(k_B\), absolute temperature \(\mathcal T\), viscosity \(\eta\), and particle radius \(r\).

title: Does a real diffusing particle justify this scaling?
context: Where the approximation stops working
text: A real particle has inertia. At times much shorter than its velocity-relaxation time, its velocity has not yet changed much, so distance scales roughly as time and squared distance as time squared. At longer times, the diffusive square-root law becomes the useful approximation. The physical crossover note retains the full inertial model and its formula.
excerpt: A real particle has inertia.

title: Give the limiting random walk a name
text: Put the construction together: keep physical time fixed, take more independent centered steps, and shrink each spatial step like the square root of its duration. The continuous limiting random path is called Brownian motion. Informally, Brownian motion is an idealized continuous random walk: it has no preferred direction; changes over disjoint time intervals have no memory of one another; and the variance of a change is proportional to its duration. It models position, not a smooth microscopic velocity.
excerpt: Put the construction together: keep physical time fixed, take more independent centered steps, and shrink each spatial step like the square root of its duration.

title: Give the limiting random walk a name
text: The central limit theorem explained the endpoint's bell curve. A stronger theorem, Donsker's invariance principle, establishes convergence of the suitably connected paths as well. We will use that result without proving it. Section 4 now turns this picture into a precise set of assumptions and asks what kind of calculus such a path will need.
excerpt: The central limit theorem explained the endpoint's bell curve.

title: Give the limiting random walk a name
context: Pause for a prediction
text: If a time step becomes four times shorter, how should a Brownian spatial step change? See the reasoning It becomes half as large: √{Δ t/4}=√{Δ t}/2. Four independent smaller steps then have the same total variance as the original step.
excerpt: If a time step becomes four times shorter, how should a Brownian spatial step change?

title: What has our coin walk become?
text: At the end of Section 3, we named the limiting picture Brownian motion. Let's describe it before writing the formal definition. Imagine watching a tiny particle in a fluid. Its position changes continuously, but each future displacement is uncertain because of unresolved kicks. Across many repeated experiments, we can predict a cloud of possible positions even though we cannot predict one particular path. Our mathematical idealization keeps that uncertainty and leaves out the very short-time inertial details. We write W(t), or equivalently W_t, for its position at time t. The letter W is conventional and gives the alternative name Wiener process.
excerpt: At the end of Section 3, we named the limiting picture Brownian motion.

title: What has our coin walk become?
text: How far does the particle move over a short interval? Recall the coin walk in Section 3: each fair toss moved exactly √{Δ t} to the right or left, so its variance was Δ t. Now watch m consecutive tosses, starting anywhere along the walk. Call the time we watch h=mΔ t. The tosses are independent, so their variances add: Var(net displacement)=m Δ t=h, standard deviation=√ h. Standard Brownian motion keeps this rule in the limit. Its net displacement from time t to time t+h is W_{t+h}-W_t. It has mean zero, and by its typical size we mean its standard deviation, √ h. For example, over 0.01 seconds the spread is 0.1; an individual path can move less or more, in either direction.
excerpt: How far does the particle move over a short interval?

title: Write down the model we have built
text: A standard Brownian motion is the normalized version of that picture. “Standard” means zero drift and variance increasing at rate one. Its assumptions are: Start at the origin: W_0=0. A Gaussian displacement over each interval: for 0\le s No memory between disjoint increments: the changes over separate, non-overlapping intervals are independent. No jumps: the position path is continuous. The path properties hold with probability one—often abbreviated “almost surely.” In \mathcal N(0,t-s), the first number is the mean and the second the variance. The standard deviation is therefore √{t-s}. Write the displacement from time s to time t as: Δ W(s,t):=W_t-W_s.
excerpt: A standard Brownian motion is the normalized version of that picture. “Standard” means zero drift and variance increasing at rate one.

title: Write down the model we have built
text: If a path has reached position 2 at time 1, its next quarter-second displacement is centered at zero with standard deviation 0.5. Its next position is consequently centered at 2. Brownian motion does not pull the particle back to the original starting point. Across fresh full experiments that all start at zero, the position distribution is centered at zero. The definition specifies how changes across time fit together. A separate bell curve at each time would not, by itself, tell us whether nearby positions belong to a continuous path or how those positions are related.
excerpt: If a path has reached position 2 at time 1, its next quarter-second displacement is centered at zero with standard deviation 0.5.

title: What can we predict about the cloud?
text: Taking s=0 in the increment law gives: \mathbb E[W_t]=0, Var(W_t)=\mathbb E[W_t^2]=t. Here \mathbb E means average across repeated experiments. The cloud keeps spreading: its standard deviation is √ t. An average of zero does not mean each individual path remains close to zero. We can also explain why the positions at two times are related. For s\le t, the later position contains all the earlier movement plus a new independent change: W_t=W_s+(W_t-W_s). Multiplying by the earlier position and averaging gives: \begin{aligned}\mathbb E[W_sW_t]&=\mathbb E[W_s^2]+\mathbb E[W_s(W_t-W_s)]\\&=s+0.\end{aligned}
excerpt: Taking \(s=0\) in the increment law gives:

title: What can we predict about the cloud?
text: The cross term is zero because the new centered change is independent of the earlier position. Since both position means are zero, this average product is their covariance: Cov(W_s,W_t)=\min\{s,t\}. Thus it is the increments, not the positions themselves, that are independent on disjoint intervals. Now compare one path with the position cloud it belongs to.
excerpt: The cross term is zero because the new centered change is independent of the earlier position.

title: Follow a path. Slice the cloud.
context: Interactive simulation experiment. What can we predict about the cloud?
text: Move the observation time. The histogram is a cross-section of the same collection of paths. Try this. Compare t=0.25 with t=1. The standard deviation doubles, rather than quadruples. Generate a new sample: individual paths change, the reference density does not. Exact Gaussian increments at a grid spacing of 0.025; straight lines only connect sampled values. The full mathematical paths remain rough between samples.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
text: Our goal is a calculus for random motion. In ordinary calculus, the next step would be to find a velocity by dividing a displacement by its duration and making the interval shorter: average velocity over [t,t+h]=\frac{W_{t+h}-W_t}{h}. For smooth motion, these slopes settle toward a finite tangent slope. For Brownian motion, we just saw that the displacement over h has standard deviation √ h. Dividing each displacement by the same duration h divides its standard deviation by h too. The spread of the slopes is therefore: \frac{√ h}{h}=\frac1{√ h}.
excerpt: Our goal is a calculus for random motion.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
text: Shorter intervals make the slopes fluctuate more strongly, rather than settle. At h=0.01 the slope's standard deviation is 10; at h=0.0001 it is 100. Its sign can go either way. This scaling suggests the rigorous result: Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable. The scaling argument is intuition for that theorem, not a proof at every point.
excerpt: Shorter intervals make the slopes fluctuate more strongly, rather than settle.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Why this matters for the calculus we want
text: We cannot treat Brownian motion as an ordinary smooth curve with a velocity W'(t). In particular, replacing a random path integral by an ordinary integral involving W'(t) will not work. We need to accumulate changes directly from the finite displacements instead.
excerpt: We cannot treat Brownian motion as an ordinary smooth curve with a velocity \(W'(t)\).

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Where does a squared displacement enter the calculation?
text: If all we want is the particle’s position, we just add its signed displacements. But earlier we also used its squared distance from the origin, W_t^2, to measure how the cloud spreads. How does that quantity change during one move? Call the current position x and the signed move δ. Subtract the old reading from the new one: \underbrace{(x+δ)^2-x^2}_{change in squared distance}=2x δ+\underbrace{δ^2}_{square of this move}.
excerpt: If all we want is the particle’s position, we just add its signed displacements.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Where does a squared displacement enter the calculation?
text: Imagine starting at x=0 and moving either +0.1 or -0.1. The slope of x^2 at zero is zero, so the linear estimate 2x δ predicts no change in either case. Yet both moves take the squared distance from zero to 0.01. The term δ^2 accounts for the whole change. For other smooth functions, a similar squared term appears wherever the graph has curvature.
excerpt: Imagine starting at \(x=0\) and moving either \(+0.1\) or \(-0.1\).

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Why do these squares disappear for smooth motion?
text: Let x(t) describe a smooth motion over a fixed duration T. Suppose its speed stays below a finite bound v_{\max}, so |x'(t)|\le v_{\max}. Divide the duration into n equal intervals, each lasting h=T/n, with t_i=ih. Call the move on interval i Δ x_i=x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i). Distance traveled is at most maximum speed times elapsed time, so: |Δ x_i|\le v_{\max}h \Longrightarrow (Δ x_i)^2\le v_{\max}^2h^2. Now add all n squared moves. There are n=T/h terms, and each is at most v_{\max}^2h^2: 0\le\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(Δ x_i)^2 \le n v_{\max}^2h^2 =\frac{T}{h} v_{\max}^2h^2 =Tv_{\max}^2h \longrightarrow0.
excerpt: Let \(x(t)\) describe a smooth motion over a fixed duration \(T\).

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Why do these squares disappear for smooth motion?
text: The duration T and speed bound v_{\max} stay fixed while h shrinks. The total is trapped between zero and a bound that shrinks to zero. For a concrete example, move at constant speed 1 for one second. With 100 intervals, the squared moves add to 100(0.01)^2=0.01. With 10,000 intervals, they add to 10{,}000(0.0001)^2=0.0001. This is why the squared contributions vanish from the accumulated change for smooth motion.
excerpt: The duration \(T\) and speed bound \(v_{\max}\) stay fixed while \(h\) shrinks.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: What stays finite for Brownian motion?
text: Use the same duration T, the same n=T/h intervals, and write Δ W_i=W_{t_{i+1}}-W_{t_i} for a move. From the Brownian increment law, each move has mean zero and variance h. Variance is the mean square minus the square of the mean, so: \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[(Δ W_i)^2] &=Var(Δ W_i)+\bigl(\mathbb E[Δ W_i]\bigr)^2\\ &=h+0^2=h. \end{aligned} Now add the squares along a path and call that total Q_n. To find its average across paths, add the average contribution of each interval: \begin{aligned} Q_n&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(Δ W_i)^2,\\ \mathbb E[Q_n] &=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathbb E[(Δ W_i)^2]\\ &=nh=\frac{T}{h} h=T. \end{aligned}
excerpt: Use the same duration \(T\), the same \(n=T/h\) intervals, and write \(\Delta W_i=W_{t_{i+1}}-W_{t_i}\) for a move.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: What stays finite for Brownian motion?
text: There are T/h terms, and each squared move contributes h on average. The factors cancel, leaving the fixed duration T even as the grid gets finer. Over one second, 100 intervals contribute 100\times0.01=1 on average. With 10,000 intervals, they still contribute 10{,}000\times0.0001=1. This is why we cannot dismiss the squared changes: their accumulated contribution stays at T on average. But an average alone does not tell us how close a particular total is to T. As we refine the grid, do the totals concentrate around that average? Section 5 answers this question by calculating their fluctuations.
excerpt: There are \(T/h\) terms, and each squared move contributes \(h\) on average.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: What stays finite for Brownian motion?
text: In Section 5’s Refine one path experiment, you can watch the squared total on finer grids of the same path. See the missing half then shows how those squares affect the change in W_t^2/2. That function is half the squared position, so each squared-change contribution is halved too. The optional regularity note discusses further path properties.
excerpt: In Section 5’s Refine one path experiment, you can watch the squared total on finer grids of the same path.

title: Can we use the usual idea of velocity?
context: Pause for a prediction
text: Are W_1 and W_2 independent? See the reasoning No. The position at time 2 includes the movement up to time 1. It is the new increment W_2-W_1 that is independent of W_1.
excerpt: Are \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) independent?

title: Add changes instead of differentiating the path
text: Section 4 gave us a problem and a way forward. Brownian motion has no ordinary velocity, so we cannot rely on a derivative W'(t). But we can still observe the position at a series of times, subtract consecutive values, and add up those finite changes. We will do three things: work out the size of a finite Brownian change, determine which products survive when many such changes are added, and use those results to build an integral and a chain rule.
excerpt: Section 4 gave us a problem and a way forward.

title: Add changes instead of differentiating the path
context: Define the time grid and its increments
text: Divide [0,T] into n equal intervals, each lasting Δ t=T/n. Write t_i=iΔ t, and use W_i as a short name for W(t_i). Then: \begin{aligned}Δ t&=t_{i+1}-t_i,\\Δ W_i&=W_{i+1}-W_i.\end{aligned} These are actual finite changes. For example, a time interval might last 0.01 seconds, and a sampled path might move from 0.3 to 0.24, giving Δ W_i=-0.06. We will also write h for the common interval length: h=Δ t=T/n. These two symbols refer to the same time step.
excerpt: Divide \([0,T]\) into \(n\) equal intervals, each lasting \(\Delta t=T/n\).

title: Add changes instead of differentiating the path
context: Derive the square-root representation
text: The Brownian increment law from Section 4 says that a displacement over duration Δ t is normal with mean zero and variance Δ t: Δ W_i\sim\mathcal N(0,Δ t). Its standard deviation is therefore √{Δ t}. To put this normal variable on a unit scale, divide it by its standard deviation and name the result Z_i: Z_i:=\frac{Δ W_i}{√{Δ t}}. Dividing by a positive constant preserves a normal distribution. Its mean remains zero, and its variance becomes: Var(Z_i)=\frac{Var(Δ W_i)}{Δ t}=1. So Z_i is a standard normal variable. Rearranging the definition gives: \boxed{Δ W_i=√{Δ t} Z_i, Z_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1).}
excerpt: The Brownian increment law from Section 4 says that a displacement over duration \(\Delta t\) is normal with mean zero and variance \(\Delta t\):

title: Add changes instead of differentiating the path
context: Derive the square-root representation
text: This is an exact finite-step relation when Z_i is defined this way. To simulate a step, reverse the procedure: draw a standard normal number and multiply it by √{Δ t}. Non-overlapping Brownian increments give independent Z_i. For Δ t=0.04, the multiplier is 0.2. A draw Z_i=0.7 produces a displacement 0.14; a draw Z_i=-1.2 produces −0.24. Unlike a single coin, a Gaussian increment can take a continuous range of values. It represents the limiting effect of many small coin-like kicks.
excerpt: This is an exact finite-step relation when \(Z_i\) is defined this way.

title: Do the squared totals concentrate around their average?
text: Section 4 found that the squared-change total has average T. We now need to know whether its fluctuations shrink as the grid gets finer. Start with the finite-step representation we just derived and square it: (Δ W_i)^2=Δ t Z_i^2. For a standard normal variable, \mathbb E[Z_i^2]=1. Thus one squared Brownian step has mean Δ t, but its actual value varies with the draw. A squared draw of 0.49 gives 0.49Δ t; a squared draw of 1.44 gives 1.44Δ t. Recall the total from Section 4: Q_n:=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(Δ W_i)^2.
excerpt: Section 4 found that the squared-change total has average \(T\).

title: Do the squared totals concentrate around their average?
text: Unlike the sum of signed moves, this total depends on the observation grid. Suppose a move of +0.2 is followed by -0.2. Observing just the start and finish gives a net move of zero and a squared-move total of 0^2=0. Observing the middle point gives the same net move, but a squared-move total of 0.2^2+(-0.2)^2=0.08. That dependence on the grid is why we ask what happens as it is refined. There are n terms, each with average Δ t, so: \mathbb E[Q_n]=nΔ t=T. An average of T alone is not enough. A quantity that is equally likely to be 0 or 2T also has average T, while remaining far from it. We need the variation of Q_n to shrink. A standard normal has fourth moment \mathbb E[Z_i^4]=3, so:
excerpt: Unlike the sum of signed moves, this total depends on the observation grid.

title: Do the squared totals concentrate around their average?
text: \begin{aligned}Var(Z_i^2)&=\mathbb E[Z_i^4]-\mathbb E[Z_i^2]^2=3-1=2,\\Var((Δ W_i)^2)&=2(Δ t)^2.\end{aligned} The squared steps are independent, so their variances add: \begin{aligned}Var(Q_n)&=n 2(Δ t)^2\\&=2TΔ t\longrightarrow0.\end{aligned} Thus the sum has mean T and a shrinking spread around T. Equivalently, its average squared error from T is: \mathbb E[(Q_n-T)^2]=2TΔ t\longrightarrow0. This is what “converges in mean square” means here: the average squared error tends to zero. The sum approaches T, even though no individual squared step becomes deterministic relative to its own size. We call the limiting accumulated squared change quadratic variation, and write [W]_T=T.
excerpt: The squared steps are independent, so their variances add:

title: Do the squared totals concentrate around their average?
text: The experiment below the three product calculations keeps one fine sampled path fixed and reveals more of its observation points. Its squared sum should settle near the elapsed duration. The sum of absolute changes measures total distance instead and keeps growing as we resolve more of the wiggles.
excerpt: The experiment below the three product calculations keeps one fine sampled path fixed and reveals more of its observation points.

title: Three accumulated products give the table
text: We will translate three accumulated-product limits into short differential rules. First calculate with finite changes; only then introduce the corresponding symbols. Observe the same journey over a fixed duration T on finer and finer grids. Each grid has n equal intervals of length h=T/n. On each interval, multiply the two changes, then add those products over the journey. All three arrows below mean convergence in mean square. For each total S_n and its proposed limit L, we check that \mathbb E[(S_n-L)^2] goes to zero. Each path supplies one total. The expectation averages its squared error across paths.
excerpt: We will translate three accumulated-product limits into short differential rules.

title: Three accumulated products give the table
context: 1. Two time increments
text: Each clock interval has length h, so every path gives exactly the same total nh^2=Th. Its ordinary numerical limit is zero. Its squared error is therefore (Th)^2 on every path. Averaging gives the very same number, which goes to zero as h shrinks. \sum_i h^2=Th\xrightarrow{mean square}0. The symbol \mathrm dt records elapsed time in differential notation. For the product of two time changes, this vanishing sum gives the shorthand: \boxed{(\mathrm dt)^2=0.} This is a limiting rule for the sum. A finite clock interval still has h^2>0.
excerpt: Each clock interval has length \(h\), so every path gives exactly the same total \(nh^2=Th\).

title: Three accumulated products give the table
context: 2. A time increment times a Brownian increment
text: Factor out the common interval length h. The signed Brownian moves add up to W_T-W_0=W_T. On any path with a finite endpoint, the total hW_T shrinks to zero. To check the same mean-square criterion as in the first row, use \mathbb E[W_T^2]=T. The average squared error is h^2\mathbb E[W_T^2]=Th^2, which goes to zero. \sum_i h Δ W_i=h\sum_i(W_{i+1}-W_i)=hW_T\xrightarrow{mean square}0. Write \mathrm dW_t for the Brownian-change differential. For its product with a time differential, the vanishing sum gives: \boxed{(\mathrm dt)(\mathrm dW_t)=(\mathrm dW_t)(\mathrm dt)=0.} The order of these scalar factors makes no difference. Again, a finite product hΔ W_i can be nonzero; it is the accumulated sum that vanishes.
excerpt: Factor out the common interval length \(h\).

title: Three accumulated products give the table
context: 3. Two Brownian increments
text: Multiply the Brownian move on each interval by itself. The finite total is Q_n, the squared-change sum we just studied. Its limit is the quadratic variation of Brownian motion: Q_n=\sum_i(Δ W_i)^2\xrightarrow{mean square}[W]_T=T. There are two different operations here. To compute Q_n, use one path and add its squared moves. To check convergence, look across paths at how far Q_n is from T. Its mean is already T on every grid. What tends to zero is the average squared error \mathbb E[(Q_n-T)^2]=2Th. This calculation holds for every ending time, so [W]_t=t. The symbol (\mathrm dW_t)^2 names the quadratic-variation contribution in Itô calculations. Its meaning is:
excerpt: Multiply the Brownian move on each interval by itself.

title: Three accumulated products give the table
context: 3. Two Brownian increments
text: \boxed{(\mathrm dW_t)^2=\mathrm d[W]_t=\mathrm dt.} Unlike the other two products, squared Brownian changes survive after summation: their limit is elapsed time. This does not make (Δ W_i)^2=h for one finite step. Now refine one path in the experiment and compare all three totals.
excerpt: Unlike the other two products, squared Brownian changes survive after summation: their limit is elapsed time.

title: Refine one path
context: Interactive simulation experiment. Three accumulated products give the table
text: Keep the underlying path fixed and add partition points. This isolates the effect of refinement. All three products use the same intervals and the same path. Compare the clock and mixed sums with the squared-noise sum, whose limit is 1 on this one-second interval. Try this. Refine from 8 to 4,096 intervals. The squared sum tends to stay near 1; the absolute sum grows. The squared sum need not move closer to 1 at every refinement. Nested dyadic partitions of one 4,096-step Gaussian sample on [0,1]. The standard deviation √{2/n} describes repeated samples, not an error bound for this particular path.
excerpt: Keep the underlying path fixed and add partition points.

title: Three accumulated products give the table
context: 3. Two Brownian increments
text: Itô multiplication table from the mean-square limits of the three sums \mathrm dt 0 0 \mathrm dW_t 0 \mathrm dt The table collects the rules we just derived. A zero records a vanishing accumulated product; \mathrm dt records the surviving quadratic variation. These symbols summarize limits of sums, rather than equalities between individual finite increments.
excerpt: Itô multiplication table from the mean-square limits of the three sums

title: Square a change, or change the square?
text: The position of the parentheses matters. Compare the two finite quantities: \begin{aligned} (Δ W_i)^2&=(W_{i+1}-W_i)^2,\\ Δ(W_i^2)&=W_{i+1}^2-W_i^2. \end{aligned} The first squares the move. The second asks how much the squared position changed. Ordinary algebra relates them: Δ(W_i^2)=2W_i Δ W_i+(Δ W_i)^2. Sum this exact identity over the grid. The changes on the left telescope: W_T^2-W_0^2=2\sum_i W_i Δ W_i+Q_n.
excerpt: The position of the parentheses matters.

title: Square a change, or change the square?
text: The notation \mathrm d(W_t^2) refers to the whole change in squared position on the left. The symbol (\mathrm dW_t)^2 refers only to the quadratic-variation contribution coming from Q_n. They are different quantities. The other term contains a changing weight W_i multiplying each move; we need an integral to describe its limit. That is our next step. After deriving the chain rule, we will return to write the full formula for \mathrm d(W_t^2).
excerpt: The notation \(\mathrm d(W_t^2)\) refers to the whole change in squared position on the left.

title: Use these changes to build an integral
text: The square identity just produced a sum in which the starting position multiplies the next move. To describe the limit of such weighted sums, first compare the two changes we can accumulate: elapsed time and signed position change.
excerpt: The square identity just produced a sum in which the starting position multiplies the next move.

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: What are we adding, and what are we integrating against?
text: Return to the move from 0.30 to 0.24 in 0.01 seconds. Two things changed during that interval: the clock advanced by 0.01, and the position changed by 0.24-0.30=-0.06. Which change do we want to accumulate? Suppose we give each change a weight of H=2, meaning we count it twice. If we are keeping track of time, we add 2\times0.01=0.02 to our total. If we are keeping track of signed movement, we add 2×(-0.06)=-0.12. The second total decreases because the particle moved to the left. Now let the weight change from one interval to the next. Call the weight at time t the integrand, H_t. On a grid of width h=T/n, we add up the contributions from every interval. The symbol at the end tells us which change to count:
excerpt: Return to the move from \(0.30\) to \(0.24\) in \(0.01\) seconds.

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: What are we adding, and what are we integrating against?
text: \begin{aligned} \sum_i H_{t_i}\underbrace{h}_{clock change} &\longrightarrow \int_0^T H_t \mathrm dt,\\ \sum_i H_{t_i}\underbrace{(W_{t_{i+1}}-W_{t_i})}_{signed position change} &\longrightarrow \int_0^T H_t \mathrm dW_t . \end{aligned}
excerpt: Use these changes to build an integral

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: What are we adding, and what are we integrating against?
text: When do we read the weight? In the Itô sum (the second line), use the weight at the start of each interval. This is its “left endpoint” on the time axis. With a constant weight of 2, the timing makes no difference. To see why it can matter, try the rule “use the particle’s current position as the weight,” so H_t=W_t. The move above starts at 0.30, so we fix the weight at 0.30. When the move ends, we can calculate its contribution: 0.30×(-0.06)=-0.018. The value 0.24 becomes available for the next interval. This is all “past-dependent” requires here: we can choose the weight using what we have seen up to and including the start.
excerpt: When do we read the weight?

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: What are we adding, and what are we integrating against?
text: What does the second arrow mean? With a changing weight, a finer grid lets us update it more often. Call the sum on n intervals S_n, and call the limiting integral I. Both depend on the path. On each path compare S_n with I for that same path, square the difference, then average across paths. Saying the sums converge in mean square means that this average error tends to zero as the grid gets finer: \mathbb E[(S_n-I)^2]\to0. What condition on the weights do we use?
excerpt: What does the second arrow mean?

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: What are we adding, and what are we integrating against?
text: We use weights whose squared sizes have a finite average when accumulated over the time interval: \mathbb E[\int_0^T H_t^2 \mathrm dt]<\infty. For H=2 this quantity is simply 4T. For the changing weights in these examples, the starting values also approximate the weights in mean square as the grid is refined. The simplest examples are just accumulated time and accumulated position change: \int_0^T1 \mathrm dt=T, \int_0^T1 \mathrm dW_t=W_T-W_0.
excerpt: We use weights whose squared sizes have a finite average when accumulated over the time interval: \(\mathbb E[\int_0^T H_t^2\,\mathrm dt]<\infty\).

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: Why does this order keep the mean at zero?
text: The next displacement is a fresh mean-zero change, independent of the past. If the multiplier is chosen before that change, its product with the next displacement has mean zero: \mathbb E[H_{t_i}Δ W_i]=0. Adding such contributions keeps the mean zero. A multiplier that uses the end of the interval would already depend on the displacement being multiplied; we will see in Section 7 that this changes the integral.
excerpt: The next displacement is a fresh mean-zero change, independent of the past.

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: How large can the accumulated integral be?
text: Square the finite sum. For a diagonal term, the future squared increment has average Δ t_i, independently of the multiplier already chosen: \mathbb E[H_{t_i}^2(Δ W_i)^2]=\mathbb E[H_{t_i}^2]Δ t_i. Cross terms from different intervals have mean zero. To see why, consider the later interval: the earlier contribution and the new multiplier have already been chosen, while the later increment is still a fresh centered change. This does not require the multipliers themselves to be independent. After summing the diagonal terms and refining the grid, we obtain the Itô isometry: \mathbb E [ (\int_0^T H_t \mathrm dW_t )^2 ]=\int_0^T\mathbb E[H_t^2] \mathrm dt.
excerpt: Square the finite sum.

title: Use these changes to build an integral
context: How large can the accumulated integral be?
text: It relates the average squared size of the random integral to an ordinary time integral. It also helps check whether approximating a multiplier gives a good approximation to its integral. For a constant multiplier H=2, the stochastic integral is 2W_T, whose variance is 4T; the right side is likewise \int_0^T4 \mathrm dt=4T.
excerpt: It relates the average squared size of the random integral to an ordinary time integral.

title: What remains familiar from ordinary calculus?
text: If the integrator is a smooth function g(t), its increments satisfy Δ g_i\approx g'(t_i)Δ t_i. The sums then recover the ordinary rule: \int_0^T H_t \mathrm dg(t)=\int_0^T H_tg'(t) \mathrm dt. For suitable finite-variation integrators and continuous multipliers, classical integration is also available. Zero quadratic variation alone is not a sufficient assumption for all such claims. When the integrator is Brownian motion but the multiplier f(t) is a smooth deterministic function of time, integration by parts gives: \int_0^T f(t) \mathrm dW_t=f(T)W_T-f(0)W_0-\int_0^T W_tf'(t) \mathrm dt.
excerpt: If the integrator is a smooth function \(g(t)\), its increments satisfy \(\Delta g_i\approx g'(t_i)\Delta t_i\).

title: What remains familiar from ordinary calculus?
text: The final term is an ordinary time integral along the sampled continuous path. When both the multiplier and the integrator depend roughly on Brownian motion, an endpoint-independent classical integral no longer supplies the answer. That is where the new product rules matter.
excerpt: The final term is an ordinary time integral along the sampled continuous path.

title: Now apply ordinary Taylor expansion to a smooth function
text: Suppose we want to know how a smooth function f(t,W_t) changes. We cannot differentiate W_t, but we can apply ordinary multivariable Taylor expansion to the finite change from (t_i,W_i) to (t_i+Δ t_i,W_i+Δ W_i): \begin{aligned}Δ f_i={}&f_tΔ t_i+f_xΔ W_i+\tfrac12f_{xx}(Δ W_i)^2\\&+f_{tx}Δ t_iΔ W_i+\tfrac12f_{tt}(Δ t_i)^2+R_i.\end{aligned} The derivatives are ordinary partial derivatives of the function f(t,x), evaluated at the start of the step, (t_i,W_i). The notation R_i collects higher-order terms. We assume enough smoothness and control of the derivatives for their summed remainders to vanish. Sum the expansion over all steps. The product table tells us what remains:
excerpt: Suppose we want to know how a smooth function \(f(t,W_t)\) changes.

title: Now apply ordinary Taylor expansion to a smooth function
text: The time-squared and time-times-Brownian products disappear. The first-order terms become a time integral and an Itô integral. The squared Brownian term survives, contributing \frac12\int f_{xx}(t,W_t) \mathrm dt.
excerpt: The time-squared and time-times-Brownian products disappear.

title: Now apply ordinary Taylor expansion to a smooth function
context: Why does the second derivative act as a multiplier?
text: Taylor expansion assigns a factor \tfrac12f_{xx}(t_i,W_i) to each squared displacement. For f(x)=x^2, that factor is the constant 1. For f(x)=x^3, it is 3W_i: the current position determines how strongly that step's square affects the function. The same averaging of squared increments works with these well-behaved starting-point factors. This is why the surviving term contains the second derivative along the path. The optional weighted-sum proof gives the mathematical details after this purpose has been established. The full integral identity is: \begin{aligned}f(T,W_T)-f(0,W_0)={}&\int_0^T (f_t+\tfrac12f_{xx} )(t,W_t) \mathrm dt\\&+\int_0^T f_x(t,W_t) \mathrm dW_t.\end{aligned}
excerpt: Taylor expansion assigns a factor \(\tfrac12f_{xx}(t_i,W_i)\) to each squared displacement.

title: Now apply ordinary Taylor expansion to a smooth function
context: Why does the second derivative act as a multiplier?
text: Using differential notation to record it gives Itô's lemma: \boxed{\mathrm df(t,W_t)= (f_t+\frac12f_{xx} )\mathrm dt+f_x \mathrm dW_t.} The extra term records the effect of curvature on many small random changes. On a convex function, symmetric up/down displacements increase the average function value. The mathematics comes from ordinary Taylor expansion plus the different size of Brownian increments.
excerpt: Using differential notation to record it gives Itô's lemma:

title: Return to the square: write the full differential
text: We already distinguished the square of a move from the change in squared position. Now use the general chain rule to find the full change. Take f(t,x)=x^2. Its derivatives are f_t=0, f_x=2x, and f_{xx}=2. Substitution gives: \begin{aligned}\mathrm d(W_t^2)&= (0+\tfrac12\times2 )\mathrm dt+2W_t \mathrm dW_t\\&=\mathrm dt+2W_t \mathrm dW_t.\end{aligned} Thus (\mathrm dW_t)^2=\mathrm dt names just the quadratic-variation term, whereas \mathrm d(W_t^2)=2W_t \mathrm dW_t+\mathrm dt includes the weighted Brownian change as well. Applying \mathrm d to the squared position is not the same operation as squaring \mathrm dW_t.

title: Return to the square: write the full differential
text: Integrate from 0 to T. Because W_0=0, the change in the square is W_T^2, and the accumulated time is T: \begin{aligned}W_T^2&=T+2\int_0^T W_t \mathrm dW_t,\\\int_0^T W_t \mathrm dW_t&=\frac12W_T^2-\frac12T.\end{aligned} Ordinary smooth-path calculus would have given just W_T^2/2. The extra -T/2 corrects for the squared displacements that did not vanish. The result also has the expected mean zero because \mathbb E[W_T^2]=T.

title: Return to the square: write the full differential

The left-endpoint contribution differs from the symmetric trapezoid contribution by a small triangular piece. Summing the identity cancels the intermediate square values: \sum_iW_iΔ W_i=\frac12W_T^2-\frac12Q_n. For smooth motion the triangular pieces vanish in total. For Brownian motion they add up to T/2. title: What does an SDE specify?
text: Section 5 supplied two tools: an integral for accumulating random changes and a chain rule for transforming them. Now we use those tools to answer one question: if we specify how a system changes locally, how can we find its evolution? We will solve a constant-coefficient equation, learn how transformations help, solve two state-dependent examples, then approximate a solution on a time grid. Itô’s lemma started with a known process W_t and computed what happens to a known function of it. In a modeling problem, we usually know a local rule for change and want to find the evolving state. This is the same shift that leads from ordinary derivatives to ordinary differential equations.
excerpt: Section 5 supplied two tools: an integral for accumulating random changes and a chain rule for transforming them.

title: What does an SDE specify?
text: An Itô stochastic differential equation specifies: \mathrm dX_t=\underbrace{a(t,X_t) \mathrm dt}_{drift}+\underbrace{b(t,X_t) \mathrm dW_t}_{diffusion}, X_0=x_0. The state is X_t, its known starting value is x_0, and W_t is the Brownian driving process. Here a(t,X_t) is the drift and b(t,X_t) is the diffusion coefficient, or noise amplitude. Over a short interval h, freeze these coefficients at the current time and state: Δ X\approx a(t,X_t)h+b(t,X_t)√ h Z, Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
excerpt: An Itô stochastic differential equation specifies:

title: What does an SDE specify?
text: Given the current state, the approximate change has mean a(t,X_t)h, variance b(t,X_t)^2h, and standard deviation \lvert b(t,X_t)\rvert√ h. So the coefficient sets the scale of a random change, not its realized size or direction. The SDE itself means: X_t=x_0+\int_0^t a(s,X_s) \mathrm ds+\int_0^t b(s,X_s) \mathrm dW_s. A solution is a process X_t satisfying that integral equation with the specified initial value and Brownian driver. Once a driving path is supplied, the solution describes the corresponding state path. A formula for that process can still contain W_t or an Itô integral: solving an SDE does not remove its randomness.
excerpt: Given the current state, the approximate change has mean \(a(t,X_t)h\), variance \(b(t,X_t)^2h\), and standard deviation \(\lvert b(t,X_t)\rvert\sqrt h\).

title: What does an SDE specify?
text: After finding the solution, we can ask for its mean and variance across repeated paths. Those statistics answer a different question from the path formula itself. Appropriate regularity and growth assumptions are needed for existence and uniqueness. Here we use familiar well-behaved examples rather than develop that theory.

title: First solve an equation with constant coefficients
text: Return to the traveler from Section 1. The clock advances by h; the traveler gains a predictable distance μ h and a random displacement σΔ W_i. Earlier we called a random displacement a “kick.” Its size varies from one interval to the next: Δ W_i=√ h Z_i, where Z_i is a standard normal draw. The noise amplitude σ\ge0 is the multiplier that controls the spread of those displacements: \mathbb E[σΔ W_i]=0, SD(σΔ W_i)=σ√ h. Thus σ is not a fixed distance traveled at each step. For the same interval h, doubling σ doubles the standard deviation of the random displacement. Meanwhile, μ is the predictable speed. Add the changes: the durations total t, and the signed random displacements telescope to σ W_t, since W_0=0.
excerpt: Return to the traveler from Section 1.

title: First solve an equation with constant coefficients
text: Δ X_i=μ h+σΔ W_i \Longrightarrow X_t=x_0+μ t+σ W_t. The spread after time t is σ√ t for σ\ge0. Here “spread” means standard deviation. Before touching the controls, predict what doubling the speed will do to that spread. In the integral notation of Section 5, the same sum reads: \begin{aligned}X_t&=x_0+\int_0^tμ \mathrm ds+\int_0^tσ \mathrm dW_s\\&=x_0+μ t+σ W_t,\\X_t&\sim\mathcal N(x_0+μ t,σ^2t).\end{aligned}

This returns to the introduction’s steady motion plus disturbances, now as a continuous model. Setting σ=0 recovers one deterministic path. Changing μ moves the mean, while changing σ changes the spread around it.

title: A tool for changing variables: Itô’s lemma
text: Direct integration worked because the coefficients were constant. If the unknown state appears in those coefficients, writing an integral can leave the unknown inside it. A change of variables may simplify that equation. This is the same strategy as solving an ordinary differential equation by substitution, but we need the stochastic chain rule. Suppose X_t obeys our SDE. Choose a smooth function f(t,x): this is the transformation rule, with x as its ordinary input. Substituting the random state X_t into that rule defines a transformed process: Y_t:=f(t,X_t).

title: A tool for changing variables: Itô’s lemma
text: So f names the function, while Y_t names its value along the process X_t. Itô’s lemma calculates the change \mathrm dY_t from the equation for \mathrm dX_t. To obtain a solution, choose a useful f, apply the lemma, integrate the simpler equation for Y_t, and undo the transformation to recover X_t. Section 5 did this for f(t,W_t). Here the state also has drift and a noise multiplier, so we first calculate its squared differential. Over a finite step, Δ X_i\approx a_iΔ t_i+b_iΔ W_i. Squaring and then using the accumulated product rules gives: (a_i h+b_iΔ W_i)^2=a_i^2h^2+2a_ib_i h Δ W_i+b_i^2(Δ W_i)^2.

title: A tool for changing variables: Itô’s lemma
text: The first two sums vanish under refinement; the last is a weighted squared-step sum, with b_i^2 known before the next Brownian increment. Its limit is \int b^2 \mathrm dt. In the shorthand of the table: (\mathrm dX_t)^2=(a \mathrm dt+b \mathrm dW_t)^2=b^2 \mathrm dt. Apply the same Taylor-sum argument to the transformed process Y_t=f(t,X_t). Its change is \mathrm dY_t=\mathrm d[f(t,X_t)], so the lemma reads: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dY_t&=\mathrm d [f(t,X_t) ]\\ &=f_t \mathrm dt+f_x \mathrm dX_t+\tfrac12f_{xx}(\mathrm dX_t)^2\\ &= (f_t+af_x+\tfrac12b^2f_{xx} )\mathrm dt+bf_x \mathrm dW_t. \end{aligned}

title: A tool for changing variables: Itô’s lemma
text: The derivatives and coefficients are evaluated at the current (t,X_t). The diffusion coefficient is squared in the correction because the correction measures local variance, not the signed fluctuation. Two examples will show how to choose f: an exponential time factor cancels a restoring drift, and a logarithm turns proportional changes into additive changes. In each case we will write down the transformation before doing the algebra.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
text: Think of a temperature fluctuating around a thermostat setting. Above the setting, the controller tends to lower it; below the setting, the controller tends to raise it. Disturbances keep pushing it away. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process is a simple model of this competition: a restoring drift proportional to the distance from a preferred level, together with constant noise amplitude. “Dynamics” means the rule describing how the state evolves: \mathrm dX_t=-θ(X_t-m) \mathrm dt+σ \mathrm dW_t, X_0=x_0, θ>0, σ\ge0. The preferred level is m; the restoring strength is θ; and σ is the noise amplitude just defined. We take the starting value x_0 to be known. When X_t>m, the drift -θ(X_t-m) is negative; when X_t

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
text: “Mean reversion” describes that restoring tendency. It does not promise that every next step moves closer to m: a random displacement can overcome the drift. Our question is: given the starting value and the Brownian driving path, what is X_t? After solving that, we will calculate its mean and variance.
excerpt: “Mean reversion” describes that restoring tendency.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Remove the preferred level, then cancel the drift
text: First measure the deviation from the preferred level: U_t=X_t-m. Since m is constant, \mathrm dU_t=\mathrm dX_t, and the equation becomes: \mathrm dU_t=-θ U_t \mathrm dt+σ \mathrm dW_t, U_0=x_0-m. Without noise, this deviation would decay as U_0e^{-θ t}. That suggests multiplying by the opposite exponential, A_t=e^{θ t}, to undo the decay. This smooth, deterministic factor has differential \mathrm dA_t=θ A_t \mathrm dt. Choose the function f(t,x)=e^{θ t}(x-m). Following the definition in the lemma, this choice gives the transformed process: Y_t=f(t,X_t)=e^{θ t}(X_t-m)=A_tU_t. We will apply Itô’s lemma to calculate \mathrm dY_t. First differentiate the function f with respect to its ordinary inputs t and x:

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Remove the preferred level, then cancel the drift
text: f_t=θ e^{θ t}(x-m), f_x=e^{θ t}, f_{xx}=0. Substitute the OU drift a=-θ(X_t-m) and diffusion coefficient b=σ into the lemma. The drift terms cancel, and the curvature correction is zero because f_{xx}=0: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dY_t &= [θ e^{θ t}(X_t-m)-θ(X_t-m)e^{θ t} +\tfrac12σ^2\cdot0 ]\mathrm dt+σ e^{θ t} \mathrm dW_t\\ &=σ e^{θ t} \mathrm dW_t. \end{aligned} This is the payoff from changing variables: the right-hand side no longer contains the unknown Y_t. Equivalently, the product rule gives the same cancellation; its mixed product vanishes because \mathrm dA_t contains only \mathrm dt, and both (\mathrm dt)^2 and (\mathrm dt)(\mathrm dW_t) vanish in the accumulated-product rules.
excerpt: Substitute the OU drift \(a=-\theta(X_t-m)\) and diffusion coefficient \(b=\sigma\) into the lemma.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Integrate, then undo the multiplication
text: Integrate the simpler equation for Y_t from zero to t: Y_t-Y_0=σ\int_0^t e^{θ s} \mathrm dW_s. Now undo the definition Y_t=A_tU_t=e^{θ t}U_t. Since A_0=1, the starting value is Y_0=U_0, giving: e^{θ t}U_t-U_0=σ\int_0^t e^{θ s} \mathrm dW_s. Multiply by e^{-θ t}. For a fixed final time t, that factor is constant with respect to the integration variable s, so it can go inside the integral: \begin{aligned} U_t&=U_0e^{-θ t}+σ\int_0^t e^{-θ t}e^{θ s} \mathrm dW_s\\ &=(x_0-m)e^{-θ t}+σ\int_0^t e^{-θ(t-s)} \mathrm dW_s. \end{aligned} Add m back to recover the state: X_t=m+(x_0-m)e^{-θ t}+σ\int_0^t e^{-θ(t-s)} \mathrm dW_s.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Integrate, then undo the multiplication
text: The first two terms describe the deterministic return toward m. The integral adds the random displacements, each weighted by how long ago it happened. A displacement at time s is multiplied by e^{-θ(t-s)}: older disturbances have had longer to fade under the restoring drift.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Calculate the mean: average the random contribution
text: Fix an observation time t. The starting value x_0, preferred level m, and coefficients are known constants. Give the random integral a name so we can follow its contribution: \begin{aligned} I_t&:=\int_0^t e^{-θ(t-s)} \mathrm dW_s,\\ X_t&=m+(x_0-m)e^{-θ t}+σ I_t. \end{aligned} The expectation averages over many Brownian paths with that same starting value. To calculate \mathbb E[I_t], return to the finite sums that define the integral. Choose 0=s_0<\cdots<s_n=t, and write: \begin{aligned} g_i&:=e^{-θ(t-s_i)}, Δ s_i:=s_{i+1}-s_i,\\ Δ W_i&:=W_{s_{i+1}}-W_{s_i},\\ I_t^{(n)}&:=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g_iΔ W_i. \end{aligned}

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Calculate the mean: average the random contribution
text: Each g_i is deterministic. Each Brownian increment has \mathbb E[Δ W_i]=0, so every finite sum has mean zero: \mathbb E[I_t^{(n)}]=\sum_i g_i \mathbb E[Δ W_i]=0. Passing from the sums to the integral needs a convergence result. The construction of the Itô integral gives mean-square convergence: \mathbb E[(I_t-I_t^{(n)})^2]\to0. This means that the expected squared approximation error vanishes. Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds the difference of the expectations: |\mathbb E[I_t]-\mathbb E[I_t^{(n)}] |\leq√{\mathbb E[(I_t-I_t^{(n)})^2]}\longrightarrow0.

title: A restoring force: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics
context: Calculate the mean: average the random contribution
text: Since every approximating expectation is zero, \mathbb E[I_t]=0. A particular path can still give a positive or negative integral. Only its average across paths vanishes. Taking the expectation of our solved OU process now gives: \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[X_t]&=m+(x_0-m)e^{-θ t}+σ \mathbb E[I_t]\\ &=m+(x_0-m)e^{-θ t}. \end{aligned} The limiting step in the mean and second-moment calculations For this fixed final time, write g(s)=e^{-θ(t-s)}. Let g_n(s)=g(s_i) on each interval [s_i,s_{i+1}). The stochastic integral of a step function is defined by its finite weighted sum, so the approximation above can be written as:

text: \begin{aligned} I_t&=\int_0^t g(s) \mathrm dW_s,\\ I_t^{(n)}&=\sum_i g(s_i)Δ W_i\\ &=\int_0^t g_n(s) \mathrm dW_s. \end{aligned} By linearity, subtracting the two integrals gives one integral of the weight error: I_t-I_t^{(n)}=\int_0^t\bigl(g(s)-g_n(s)\bigr) \mathrm dW_s. Now apply the Itô isometry from Section 5. For a square-integrable integrand H_s, it states: \mathbb E [ (\int_0^t H_s \mathrm dW_s )^2 ] =\mathbb E [\int_0^t H_s^2 \mathrm ds ]. Here choose H_s=g(s)-g_n(s). Substituting this particular integrand shows each step:

Therefore \mathbb E[Δ W_iΔ W_j]=\mathbb E[Δ W_i]\mathbb E[Δ W_j]=0. Each squared term has \mathbb E[(Δ W_i)^2]=Δ s_i, its interval's duration. The result is:

As s runs from zero to t, r runs from t down to zero, and \mathrm ds=-\mathrm dr:
