title: Multiplicative noise: geometric Brownian motion
text: Imagine a positive quantity whose changes are naturally expressed as percentages, such as a simplified asset value. If the current value doubles, the same percentage move produces twice the absolute change. Both its trend and its random disturbances can therefore scale with its current size. Geometric Brownian motion (GBM) models that proportional change using Brownian noise. The OU model pulled toward a preferred level with a fixed absolute noise amplitude. GBM has proportional drift and proportional noise, and its positive starting value stays positive under the model: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dS_t&=μ S_t \mathrm dt+σ S_t \mathrm dW_t,\\ S_0&>0, σ\geq0. \end{aligned}
excerpt: Imagine a positive quantity whose changes are naturally expressed as percentages, such as a simplified asset value.

title: Multiplicative noise: geometric Brownian motion
text: Here S_t is the value, μ is its constant relative drift rate, and σ is its relative noise amplitude, often called volatility. Dividing by the current value exposes the local percentage-change rule: \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS_t}{S_t}&=μ \mathrm dt+σ \mathrm dW_t,\\ \frac{Δ S_t}{S_t}&\approxμ h+σ√ h Z, Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1). \end{aligned} Over a short interval h, the relative change has approximate mean μ h and standard deviation σ√ h. The absolute random change has standard deviation approximately σ S_t√ h. There is no preferred level m pulling the value back. Constant coefficients and continuous paths make this an idealized model.
excerpt: Here \(S_t\) is the value, \(\mu\) is its constant relative drift rate, and \(\sigma\) is its relative noise amplitude, often called volatility.

title: Multiplicative noise: geometric Brownian motion
context: Use a logarithm to turn proportional changes into additive changes
text: A logarithm turns multiplication into addition, which suggests the transformation. For this example choose f(t,x)=\log x on x>0, and define its value along S_t: \begin{aligned} Y_t&=f(t,S_t)=\log S_t,\\ f_t&=0, f_x=\frac1x, f_{xx}=-\frac1{x^2}. \end{aligned} Apply the same Itô lemma, using S_t as the state. Its squared differential is (\mathrm dS_t)^2=σ^2S_t^2 \mathrm dt, so: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dY_t&=\mathrm d[\log S_t]\\ &=\frac1{S_t} \mathrm dS_t-\frac1{2S_t^2}(\mathrm dS_t)^2\\ &=μ \mathrm dt+σ \mathrm dW_t-\frac12σ^2 \mathrm dt\\ &= (μ-\frac{σ^2}{2} )\mathrm dt+σ \mathrm dW_t. \end{aligned}
excerpt: A logarithm turns multiplication into addition, which suggests the transformation.

title: Multiplicative noise: geometric Brownian motion
context: Use a logarithm to turn proportional changes into additive changes
text: The equation for the log-value now has constant coefficients, just like our first solved example. Itô's lemma supplied this transformed equation. Integrate it, then exponentiate to recover S_t: \begin{aligned} Y_t-Y_0=\log S_t-\log S_0&= (μ-\frac{σ^2}{2} )t+σ W_t,\\ S_t&=S_0\exp [ (μ-\frac{σ^2}{2} )t+σ W_t ]. \end{aligned} This exponential form explains the word “geometric”: additive changes in the log-value become multiplicative changes in the value. It also shows why S_t stays positive when S_0>0.
excerpt: The equation for the log-value now has constant coefficients, just like our first solved example.

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
text: We have a formula for each path. As with OU, the next step is to interpret its distribution at an observation time t. Since W_t\sim\mathcal N(0,t), the log-value is Gaussian: \log S_t\sim\mathcal N (\log S_0+ (μ-\frac{σ^2}{2} )t,\ σ^2t ). A positive variable with a Gaussian logarithm is called lognormal. For positive noise at positive time, its distribution is skewed toward large values. The mean averages the values across repeated runs; the median marks the halfway point in probability. Large outcomes can raise the average even when more than half of the outcomes lie below it.
excerpt: We have a formula for each path.

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
context: Calculate the mean by averaging the exponential noise
text: At a fixed time, take the deterministic factors outside the expectation. The exponential of the Brownian term remains inside: \mathbb E[S_t]=S_0e^{(μ-σ^2/2)t} \mathbb E[e^{σ W_t}]. A zero-mean Brownian value does not make this exponential factor average to one. The Gaussian exponential moment is \mathbb E[e^{σ W_t}]=e^{σ^2t/2}. Substituting it cancels the negative half-variance term: \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[S_t]&=S_0e^{(μ-σ^2/2)t}e^{σ^2t/2}\\ &=S_0e^{μ t}. \end{aligned} The Gaussian exponential moment Write W_t=√ t Z, where Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1), and put c=σ√ t. Complete the square in the Gaussian density:
excerpt: At a fixed time, take the deterministic factors outside the expectation.

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
context: Calculate the mean by averaging the exponential noise
text: \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[e^{cZ}]&=\frac1{√{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{cz-z^2/2} \mathrm dz\\ &=e^{c^2/2}\frac1{√{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(z-c)^2/2} \mathrm dz\\ &=e^{c^2/2}. \end{aligned} The remaining integral is a normal density with mean c, so it integrates to one. Taking c=σ√ t gives the factor used above.
excerpt: The remaining integral is a normal density with mean \(c\), so it integrates to one.

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
context: Calculate the median from the halfway probability
text: For t>0 and σ>0, Brownian symmetry gives \mathbb P(W_t\leq0)=1/2. The exponential is strictly increasing, so values below the zero-noise term inside the exponential correspond exactly to Brownian values below zero: \begin{aligned} &\mathbb P (S_t\leq S_0e^{(μ-σ^2/2)t} )\\ & =\mathbb P(σ W_t\leq0)=\frac12. \end{aligned} That identifies the median directly: median(S_t)=S_0e^{(μ-σ^2/2)t}. At each observation time, half the values lie below this level and half above it. This calculation follows the middle probability through an increasing transformation. The mean required averaging the exponential itself. With zero noise, both summaries reduce to the same deterministic value S_0e^{μ t}; at t=0, both equal S_0.
excerpt: For \(t>0\) and \(\sigma>0\), Brownian symmetry gives \(\mathbb P(W_t\leq0)=1/2\).

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
context: Connect the two summaries to the plotted growth
text: The mean grows at exponential rate μ; the median grows at rate μ-σ^2/2. When 0<μ<σ^2/2, the mean rises while the median falls. This is a consequence of the distribution's asymmetry and explains why the average alone can give an incomplete description of the model's outcomes.
excerpt: The mean grows at exponential rate \(\mu\); the median grows at rate \(\mu-\sigma^2/2\).

title: Read the GBM solution: mean and median
context: Connect the two summaries to the plotted growth
text: Interpreting an investment projection. GBM is used as a simple model of asset prices with proportional random changes. Under the condition just described, expected wealth grows even though more than half the possible outcomes finish below the initial investment: large gains in the upper tail lift the average. A high expected value therefore does not imply a high chance of making a gain. The median locates the middle outcome; assessing a particular goal also requires the probability of a loss or of reaching a target. These are implications of the model, whose assumptions must be assessed for the asset being studied.
excerpt: Interpreting an investment projection.

title: When a transformation does not give an explicit solution
text: We chose two particularly helpful substitutions. For a general SDE there may be no similarly useful explicit formula. We can still approximate its evolution by freezing the coefficients at the start of each short interval. This is the Euler–Maruyama method: X_{i+1}=X_i+a(t_i,X_i)h+b(t_i,X_i)Δ W_i, Δ W_i=√ h Z_i, Z_i\stackrel{iid}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1). Start with the known X_0=x_0, evaluate the drift and noise amplitude there, draw the next Brownian increment, and update. Repeat with the new state. The output is a numerical approximation at the grid times. Test this method on OU, where we already have an exact answer. For m=0, its Euler update is: X_{i+1}^{Euler}=(1-θ h)X_i^{Euler}+σΔ W_i.

title: What have we learned to do?
text: An SDE specifies local drift and random variation. A solution describes the resulting process. Itô’s lemma describes a transformed process and can help us find a solution. Euler–Maruyama approximates paths when we work on a grid. The three earlier experiments use exact sampled solutions; the final experiment deliberately introduces numerical error so we can study it. title: From smooth forcing to symmetric accumulation
text: Section 6 chose the noise coefficient before each next Brownian increment. Now consider another starting point: an ordinary differential equation responding continuously to a smooth, rapidly varying driving signal. As the signal becomes rougher, which stochastic equation retains that response? Start with a smooth signal w(t). Ordinary calculus gives: \int_0^T w(t) \mathrm dw(t)=\frac12\bigl(w(T)^2-w(0)^2\bigr). Join successive Brownian readings W_i and W_{i+1} with a straight segment. Along that segment, the signal changes continuously, so its ordinary integral uses the average of the endpoint values:
excerpt: Section 6 chose the noise coefficient before each next Brownian increment.

title: From smooth forcing to symmetric accumulation
text: \begin{aligned} segment contribution &=\frac{W_i+W_{i+1}}2 (W_{i+1}-W_i)\\ &= (W_i+\frac12Δ W_i )Δ W_i. \end{aligned} This suggests symmetric accumulation: include the multiplier's change during the increment, rather than freeze it at the start. Its Brownian limit is the Stratonovich integral, written \circ \mathrm dW. The evaluation rule changes the multiplier used for each contribution; the integration bounds remain 0 and T. From smooth driving signals to the Wong–Zakai limit Let W^\varepsilon be standard piecewise-linear approximations to Brownian motion, and solve an ordinary equation before taking the limit: \dot x^\varepsilon=\widetilde a(x^\varepsilon)+b(x^\varepsilon)\dot W^\varepsilon.
excerpt: This suggests symmetric accumulation: include the multiplier's change during the increment, rather than freeze it at the start.

title: From smooth forcing to symmetric accumulation
text: Under suitable coefficient regularity and convergence assumptions, the limiting equation is \mathrm dX=\widetilde a(X) \mathrm dt+b(X)\circ\mathrm dW. This is the classical Wong–Zakai connection. It motivates a continuously responding system's equation without treating the noise coefficient as frozen over each segment. The approximation mechanism matters, especially with several driving signals. A physical noise source does not universally select one convention. Kelly and Melbourne, Smooth approximation of stochastic differential equations, discuss the assumptions and extensions.
excerpt: Under suitable coefficient regularity and convergence assumptions, the limiting equation is \(\mathrm dX=\widetilde a(X)\,\mathrm dt+b(X)\circ\mathrm dW\).

title: The Brownian correction survives
text: On the same step, compare Itô's left-value contribution with the symmetric contribution. Their difference is a squared increment: \begin{aligned} left contribution&=W_iΔ W_i,\\ symmetric contribution&= (W_i+\frac12Δ W_i )Δ W_i,\\ difference&=\frac12(Δ W_i)^2. \end{aligned} For a smooth path, the sum of squared increments vanishes as the grid is refined. For Brownian motion, Section 5 showed that Q_n:=\sum_i(Δ W_i)^2→ T in mean square. Thus the accumulated difference approaches T/2, even though each step becomes tiny. With W_0=0, the symmetric terms telescope to W_T^2/2. The two limits are therefore:
excerpt: On the same step, compare Itô's left-value contribution with the symmetric contribution.

title: The Brownian correction survives
text: \begin{aligned} \int_0^T W_t \mathrm dW_t&=\frac12(W_T^2-T),\\ \int_0^T W_t\circ\mathrm dW_t&=\frac12W_T^2. \end{aligned} The circle records a different accumulation rule on the same Brownian path. The symmetric rule retains the term that makes the ordinary chain rule work. It does not describe a trader choosing a holding with knowledge of the next price change.

title: The Brownian correction survives
text: For example, the grid \{0,0.2,0.7,1\} has a mesh of 0.5, the length of the interval from 0.2 to 0.7. Taking |\pi|\to0 means refining the grid so that even its longest interval tends to zero. The steps may have different lengths. For continuous semimartingales and suitable integrability, the Stratonovich integral is the limit in probability of symmetric integrand-endpoint sums: \int_0^T H_t\circ\mathrm dW_t =\lim_{|\pi|\to0}\sum_i\frac{H_{t_i}+H_{t_{i+1}}}{2}Δ W_i. For a smooth state-dependent integrand, evaluating it at the average of the endpoint states gives the same limit in the setting considered here. Neither expression says that the actual Brownian path follows the straight segment between its readings.

title: The Brownian correction survives
text: For a smooth function f(t,x) of a continuous diffusion X_t, the symmetric contribution absorbs Itô's curvature correction, giving: \mathrm d[f(t,X_t)]=f_t(t,X_t) \mathrm dt+f_x(t,X_t)\circ\mathrm dX_t. This is the ordinary chain rule in Stratonovich notation. The quadratic variation is still present; it is included in the symmetric integral rather than written as a separate second-derivative term.

title: Translate the equation, preserve the process
text: Different integral values do not prevent equivalent descriptions of one process. The drift must compensate for the change in accumulation. Return to Section 6's multiplicative model, with constants μ,σ and the same positive starting value X_0. Itô: \mathrm dX=μ X \mathrm dt+σ X \mathrm dW X_t=X_0e^{(μ-σ^2/2)t+σ W_t} Stratonovich: \mathrm dX=μ X \mathrm dt+σ X\circ\mathrm dW X_t=X_0e^{μ t+σ W_t} The second solution follows by applying the ordinary chain rule to \log X, integrating, then exponentiating. It differs from the first solution. To preserve the first process, subtract σ^2X/2 from the Stratonovich drift:
excerpt: Different integral values do not prevent equivalent descriptions of one process.

title: Translate the equation, preserve the process
text: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dX&=μ X \mathrm dt+σ X \mathrm dW &&(Itô),\\ \mathrm dX&= (μ-\frac{σ^2}{2} )X \mathrm dt+σ X\circ\mathrm dW &&(Stratonovich). \end{aligned} These descriptions produce the same path for the same Brownian driver. As with Newtonian, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, equivalent formulations can expose different useful structures. Here, changing the integral convention requires translating the drift as well.

title: Translate the equation, preserve the process
text: The stochastic part of Δ X_i is b(t_i,X_i)Δ W_i. Its product with Δ W_i survives summation through Brownian squared increments; drift–noise products vanish. Under the usual smoothness and localization assumptions, the correction is \tfrac12\int b \partial_xb \mathrm dt. a_{\mathrm I}(t,x)=a_{\mathrm S}(t,x)+\frac12b(t,x)\partial_xb(t,x). Here a_{\mathrm I} is the Itô drift and a_{\mathrm S} the Stratonovich drift. For b(t,x)=σ x, their difference is σ^2x/2. For additive noise b=b(t), the spatial derivative is zero. Several state variables or Brownian drivers require the appropriate vector-field correction, not a copied scalar formula. See Evans, pp. 111–115.
excerpt: The stochastic part of \(\Delta X_i\) is \(b(t_i,X_i)\Delta W_i\).

title: Choose the form that fits the calculation
text: Once the model is specified, either convention can describe it after conversion. Itô form is convenient when the coefficient is chosen using current information: its Brownian integral has mean zero under square-integrability, and the isometry supports variance calculations. Those are the tools used for OU in Section 6. Stratonovich form is convenient when deriving a model from suitable smooth driving signals or changing coordinates: the usual chain rule keeps that structure visible. This does not remove noise-induced drift effects; conversion makes them explicit in Itô form.
excerpt: Once the model is specified, either convention can describe it after conversion.

title: Choose the form that fits the calculation
text: Section 6 already contains the distinction. OU has constant noise coefficient b=σ, so changing convention leaves its drift unchanged. GBM has b=σ x, so its equivalent descriptions differ by σ^2x/2. The system's mechanism determines the model; the preferred form then depends on the calculation. Optional applications: coordinates, control and varying diffusivity A coordinate change can preserve a useful expression for a model. For a scalar controlled equation, with control input u_t: \begin{aligned} \mathrm dX&=(aX+u_t) \mathrm dt+σ X\circ\mathrm dW,\\ \mathrm d(X^2)&=(2aX^2+2Xu_t) \mathrm dt+2σ X^2\circ\mathrm dW. \end{aligned}
excerpt: Section 6 already contains the distinction.

title: Choose the form that fits the calculation
text: The equivalent Itô drift is (a+σ^2/2)X+u_t; Itô's formula gives the same evolution of X^2. A convenient expression does not itself supply a stabilizing control. For a second application, suppose a concentration density p(t,x) is intended to obey Fick's law with positive position-dependent diffusivity D(x): \partial_tp=\partial_x(D \partial_xp). The density equation shows that its scalar Itô representation has b=√{2D} and drift a_{\mathrm I}=D'. Since b b'=D', the same model has Stratonovich drift D'/2. In the right-endpoint convention introduced next, its written drift is zero. The desired transport law is the premise here; not every heterogeneous medium must follow it.
excerpt: The equivalent Itô drift is \((a+\sigma^2/2)X+u_t\); Itô's formula gives the same evolution of \(X^2\).

title: Beyond two conventions: the λ-family
text: Itô and Stratonovich cover two important accumulation rules, but some effective models need intermediate corrections. In a noisy electrical circuit, researchers varied the relation between the noise's correlation time—how long a fluctuation remains related to its past—and the feedback delay—how long the circuit takes to respond. They observed a continuous transition from Stratonovich toward Itô behavior, passing through intermediate conventions. Pesce and colleagues, Stratonovich-to-Itô transition in noisy systems with multiplicative feedback (2013).
excerpt: Itô and Stratonovich cover two important accumulation rules, but some effective models need intermediate corrections.

title: Beyond two conventions: the λ-family
text: The λ-family provides one scalar notation for such rules. For our linear example, use W_i+λΔ W_i as the multiplier. Itô is λ=0, Stratonovich is λ=1/2, and the right-endpoint or Hänggi–Klimontovich convention is λ=1. \begin{aligned} I_{λ,n} &=\sum_i(W_i+λΔ W_i)Δ W_i\\ &=\frac12W_T^2+ (λ-\frac12 )Q_n,\\ I_λ&=\frac12W_T^2+ (λ-\frac12 )T. \end{aligned} The first identity is exact on the finite grid; the second expression is its mean-square limit. Since \mathbb E[W_T^2]=T, its expectation is \mathbb E[I_λ]=λ T. This family changes the integral on a fixed path. To preserve an SDE's process, compensate its drift.
excerpt: The \(\lambda\)-family provides one scalar notation for such rules.

title: Beyond two conventions: the λ-family
text: The symbol \diamond_λ labels the convention. Here λ interpolates between endpoint states; it does not select the actual Brownian reading at physical time t_i+λΔ t_i. For smooth g, the midpoint-state rule has the same limit as the symmetric integrand-endpoint definition. If X has noise coefficient b(t,X_t), Taylor expansion about the left state gives: \begin{aligned} g(X_i+λΔ X_i)Δ W_i &=g(X_i)Δ W_i\\ & +λ g'(X_i)Δ X_iΔ W_i+remainder. \end{aligned} The surviving squared-increment sum comes from Δ X_iΔ W_i\approx b(t_i,X_i)(Δ W_i)^2. Under suitable smoothness, moment and localization assumptions, the remainder vanishes in probability, yielding:
excerpt: The symbol \(\diamond_\lambda\) labels the convention.

title: Beyond two conventions: the λ-family
text: \begin{aligned} \int_0^Tg(X_t)\diamond_λ\mathrm dW_t &=\int_0^Tg(X_t) \mathrm dW_t\\ & +λ\int_0^Tg'(X_t)b(t,X_t) \mathrm dt. \end{aligned} Putting g=b, with any time dependence evaluated at the same time, gives the equivalent scalar drift: \begin{aligned} a_{\mathrm I}&=a_λ+λ b \partial_xb,\\ a_{\lambda_1}-a_{\lambda_2} &=(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)b \partial_xb. \end{aligned} For a smooth f(t,x), the matching chain rule is: \begin{aligned} \mathrm d[f(t,X_t)] &= (f_t+ (\frac12-λ )b^2f_{xx} )\mathrm dt\\ & +f_x\diamond_λ\mathrm dX_t. \end{aligned}

title: Beyond two conventions: the λ-family
text: For a fixed process, changing λ and its drift together is a translation. Relative to a specified underlying drift, a parameter inferred from a microscopic limit can instead encode a noise-induced correction. An unconstrained drift and λ cannot be identified separately from this scalar effective equation alone.
excerpt: For a fixed process, changing \(\lambda\) and its drift together is a translation.

title: Make the numerical method match the model
text: Section 6 used Euler–Maruyama, which evaluates coefficients at the beginning of each step and targets the Itô equation. Giving it an unconverted Stratonovich drift generally simulates a different model. For the equivalent multiplicative equations above, use the Itô drift μ X with Euler–Maruyama. A suitable Stratonovich method instead uses the drift (μ-σ^2/2)X. The convention, coefficients and numerical method must describe the same equation. Scalar midpoint and Heun steps For a scalar Stratonovich equation with drift \widetilde a and noise coefficient b, an implicit midpoint step uses the average of the starting and ending states:
excerpt: Section 6 used Euler–Maruyama, which evaluates coefficients at the beginning of each step and targets the Itô equation.

title: Make the numerical method match the model
text: \begin{aligned} X_{n+1}&=X_n+\widetilde a (\frac{X_n+X_{n+1}}2 )Δ t\\ & +b (\frac{X_n+X_{n+1}}2 )Δ W_n. \end{aligned} It is implicit because the unknown endpoint appears on both sides. A common explicit Heun predictor–corrector first predicts an endpoint, then averages coefficients using that prediction. title: Use a valve log to estimate the Brownian noise level

If the valve stayed closed, Brownian motion alone had to produce -0.50, a fall of five standard deviations. title: Use a valve log to estimate the Brownian noise level

Multiply those odds by the likelihood ratio to get about 163:1 in favor of an opening, or a probability of about 99.4\%. If openings occur in only one out of a million comparable minutes, the same calculation gives about 14\%. The pressure reading supplies the same evidence in both cases. title: What did we learn from the four experiments?
text: In Example 1, a straight-line regression predicted the average next reading, and the residuals told us how much one reading could vary. title: Optional note: the physical crossover to diffusion
text: Section 3 uses the observed/modelled spreading law to motivate the coin-walk scaling. A more detailed equilibrium inertial model keeps velocity as well as position: m \mathrm dV_t=-\gamma V_t \mathrm dt+√{2\gamma k_B\mathcal T} \mathrm dW_t, \mathrm dX_t=V_t \mathrm dt. With stationary initial velocity, define the relaxation time \tau=m/\gamma and diffusivity D=k_B\mathcal T/\gamma. Integrating the stationary velocity covariance gives: \mathbb E[(X_t-X_0)^2]=2D [t-\tau(1-e^{-t/\tau}) ].
excerpt: Section 3 uses the observed/modelled spreading law to motivate the coin-walk scaling.

title: Optional note: the physical crossover to diffusion
text: For t\ll\tau, expand the exponential to obtain approximately (D/\tau)t^2, the ballistic regime. For t\gg\tau, the leading term is 2Dt, the diffusive regime. The relaxation time depends on the particle and fluid. This distinguishes the continuous Brownian position model from the microscopic inertial motion it approximates.
excerpt: For \(t\ll\tau\), expand the exponential to obtain approximately \((D/\tau)t^2\), the ballistic regime.

title: Optional note: Brownian path regularity
text: The main lesson explains the consequence needed for calculus: Brownian paths have no ordinary derivative, and their squared changes accumulate. More technically, the Gaussian fourth moment is \mathbb E[|W_t-W_s|^4]=3|t-s|^2. The usual continuity arguments give versions whose paths, on bounded time intervals, are Hölder continuous of every order \alpha<1/2. They are not uniformly 1/2-Hölder on any nontrivial interval; the borderline behavior involves logarithmic corrections. Brownian paths have infinite total variation. On a uniform partition, one illustrative calculation is: \mathbb E [\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}|Δ W_i| ]=n√{\frac{2Δ t}{\pi}}=√{\frac{2Tn}{\pi}}.
excerpt: The main lesson explains the consequence needed for calculus: Brownian paths have no ordinary derivative, and their squared changes accumulate.

title: Optional note: why starting-point weights preserve the squared-step rule
text: Taylor expansion in Section 5 creates the weights: the factor \tfrac12 f_{xx}(t_i,W_i) changes with the starting point of the step. This is why we need a weighted version of quadratic variation. For bounded coefficients G_i determined before the next increment, write the difference between a weighted squared-step sum and its time-step counterpart as: R_n=\sum_iG_i\bigl[(Δ W_i)^2-Δ t\bigr]. Each bracket has conditional mean zero given the past. Consequently cross expectations between different intervals vanish, and the mean square of the difference is: \mathbb E[R_n^2]=2(Δ t)^2\sum_i\mathbb E[G_i^2]\longrightarrow0.

title: Optional note: why starting-point weights preserve the squared-step rule
text: The boundedness assumption makes the last expression at most a constant times TΔ t. If the time sums converge to an ordinary integral, the weighted squared sums have the same limit. Unbounded cases require suitable integrability or localization. These qualifications support the calculus derivation; they are not prerequisites for understanding the finite-step examples in the main text. The vanishing product rules also tolerate bounded starting-point weights. For |G_i|\le C, the weighted time-squared sum has absolute value at most CTΔ t. By the finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the weighted mixed sum satisfies: |\sum_iG_iΔ t Δ W_i |\le C√{\sum_i(Δ t)^2}√{\sum_i(Δ W_i)^2}=C√{TΔ t}√{Q_n}\longrightarrow0.
excerpt: The boundedness assumption makes the last expression at most a constant times \(T\Delta t\).

title: Optional note: why starting-point weights preserve the squared-step rule
text: For the square-integrable Itô integral, a formal construction uses suitably measurable, past-dependent integrands with \mathbb E[\int_0^T H_t^2 \mathrm dt]<\infty, first defines elementary sums, and extends them using the isometry. For the derivation, enough smoothness to control Taylor remainders is convenient. Itô's formula extends to C^{1,2} functions under the usual local conditions.

title: Optional note: symbolic stochastic differentiation
text: One algebraic representation of the retained orders uses \mathbb R[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^3), identifying \varepsilon with a formal noise increment and \varepsilon^2 with the time contribution. This extends the dual-number idea used in ordinary automatic differentiation. It is a representation of the multiplication rules, not a replacement for constructing the stochastic integral. The source author explores this approach in Automatic Stochastic Differentiation.
